clue.text: Galvanise York, say, almost swamped by river

indicators.note: swamped means covered on all sides, so the river's letters close round the shortened city

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, a crossword regular

indicators.note: almost means the last letter of the city word is dropped

parts.note: York is an example of a city

explanation.surface: Someone tries to stir up York, a city nearly flooded by its river.
explanation.walkthrough: York is merely an example of a city; the river is the Exe in Devon, not York's own Ouse.
explanation.definitionFit: To galvanise is to rouse or stimulate into action, a close synonym.

clue.text: You've reached the limit? Then it is what it is!

definitions.text: You've reached the limit? Then it is what it is!

parts.words: You've reached the limit? Then it is what it is!
parts.note: a shouted word meaning 'stop now', said when patience is exhausted, and also a word for a sufficient amount

explanation.surface: A weary shrug: once you've hit the limit, there's nothing to be done.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue plays on the idiom 'enough is enough': at the limit, the word simply is itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Reaching the limit means having as much as is sufficient, so no more is wanted.

clue.text: Decoration of a capital city? Something fraudulent about it

indicators.note: about means the swindle word goes round the article and the city

parts.note: a con is a swindle, something fraudulent
Paris is the capital city of France

explanation.surface: Asks whether a capital's ornamentation is a fraud surrounding it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' points back to 'a capital city', which the swindle word goes round.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an ornamental cloth covering for a horse, so a piece of decoration or finery.

clue.text: Char comes into this parlour

parts.note: char is British slang for tea, which is served in this room; a char is also a cleaning lady

explanation.surface: A cleaning lady arrives at work in a sitting room.
explanation.walkthrough: Char is British slang for tea (and also a charwoman, a cleaner), so the parlour is one where tea is served.
explanation.definitionFit: A small cafe serving tea and cakes is a parlour where cups of tea arrive.

clue.text: Supplied with a grave?

parts.note: a grave is also the backward-sloping accent mark over a vowel, so a letter given one has a mark added

explanation.surface: Someone or something has been provided with a burial plot.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a tomb; the grave here is the accent in words like 'à la'.
explanation.definitionFit: A vowel given a grave mark carries a diacritic, so it has been marked with stress.

clue.text: Test Rubicon somehow presents

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters are put together in some unspecified new arrangement

explanation.surface: A trial crossing of Caesar's Rubicon river shows up in some form.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rubicon is the river Caesar crossed; its letters with TEST rearrange fully to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To present a gift or offering is to give it, as one gives towards a collection.

clue.text: Occupants of Lambeth I call 'principled'

indicators.note: Occupants of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone describes the residents of Lambeth, a London borough, as people of principle.
explanation.walkthrough: Lambeth is a London borough, home to Lambeth Palace of the Archbishop of Canterbury.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting according to moral standards makes someone principled; both are adjectives of good conduct.

clue.text: Moved round without resistance — fit to play?

indicators.note: without means the resistance letter is taken away

parts.note: turned means rotated, moved round
R is the physics symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A player rotated freely and was declared match-fit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes R (resistance) from TURNED. The definition refers to an instrument ready to play, not an athlete.
explanation.definitionFit: An instrument set to correct pitch is ready, fit to play.

clue.text: Suffering of duke with lover heading off

indicators.note: heading off means the first letter of the lover word is lost

parts.note: a mistress is a lover

explanation.surface: A duke's lover leaves, causing him pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' drops the first letter of MISTRESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Anguish or pain is meant; both name mental or physical suffering.

clue.text: Some indoor phantom appears for unfortunate child

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A ghost inside the house turns up in place of a hapless youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'appears for' into the definition; it is only a link joining wordplay to definition, so the definition is 'unfortunate child'.
explanation.definitionFit: A youngster who has lost both parents is pitied as an unfortunate child.

clue.text: Leaders of English nature club wanting Hampshire delights

indicators.note: the leaders of the words are their opening letters, taken from English, nature and club

parts.note: Hants is the standard abbreviation for the English county of Hampshire

explanation.surface: An English wildlife society needs members from Hampshire, a county in southern England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaders of' takes the first letters of English, nature and club; HANTS is the usual short form of Hampshire.
explanation.definitionFit: To delight someone is to charm or captivate them, which is the verb's sense here.

clue.text: Murderer good? A right baddie!

parts.note: a rotter is an old-fashioned word for a cad or villain

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a killer is good, then answers that he is a real villain.
explanation.definitionFit: This is someone who kills by strangling with a cord or wire, a kind of killer.

clue.text: This base man wanders around riverside region

indicators.note: wanders around suggests these letters move about into a new order

explanation.surface: A lowly man drifts about near a riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanders around' rearranges THIS BASE MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The land drained by London's river is a region lying along its banks.

clue.text: Detectives attending the Queen drink

parts.note: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the British police detective branch
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, Queen Elizabeth

explanation.surface: Police detectives escorting the monarch take a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: CID is the plain-clothes detective branch of British police; ER is the royal cipher of Queen Elizabeth.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an alcoholic drink made from fermented apples, so a type of drink.

clue.text: People walking out for the count?

definitions.text: People walking out for the count?

parts.words: People walking out for the count?
parts.note: out for the count means fast asleep, and these people walk about while still asleep

explanation.surface: It sounds like folk striding out to be counted, or boxers flattened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out for the count' is boxing slang for knocked out, used loosely for being deeply asleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleepwalkers move about while unconscious in sleep, so they walk while out cold.

clue.text: Employer of agents unusually smart, yes? Must keep quiet!

indicators.note: keep means the shuffled letters hold the quiet letter within them
unusually signals the letters of smart and yes are arranged differently

parts.note: P, for piano, is the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: A boss of spies is unusually sharp and must stay silent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusually' rearranges SMART YES, and 'keep' puts P (piano, quiet) inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The head of an espionage network directs, and so employs, secret agents.

clue.text: Well-off ace, loud and articulate

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for ace in cards
F, for forte, is the musical direction for loud
fluent means articulate, speaking smoothly

explanation.surface: Describes someone rich, brilliant, loud and well-spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Wealthy and prosperous are synonyms for well-off.

clue.text: 'Money has the last word' — agree in essence?

parts.note: a fund is a sum of money set aside
amen is said at the very end of a prayer, so it is the last word
to tally is to agree or correspond

explanation.surface: A cynic claims money always wins the argument, asking whether that is basically agreed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Amen' closes prayers, so it is 'the last word'.
explanation.definitionFit: Basically and at heart mean the same as in essence; the adverb fits the phrase.

clue.text: Analyst — idiot always right

parts.note: an ass is a fool
aye is an old or poetic word for always

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at an analyst as a fool who's never wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: AYE (also spelt 'ay') is an archaic word for ever or always.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone testing metals or ores for purity is a kind of chemical analyst.

clue.text: Group of stars given censure before beginning to receive thanks

parts.note: to lace into someone is to attack or rebuke them; lace can mean thrash or censure

indicators.note: beginning to picks the opening letter of receive

parts.note: ta is British informal for thank you

explanation.surface: Someone gets reprimanded just before being thanked.
explanation.walkthrough: TA is everyday British slang for thanks. LACE for censure is a stretch, from 'lace into'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the name of a small northern constellation, the Lizard, so a group of stars.

clue.text: Not upright as a character

parts.note: a sloping typeface is not upright, the character being a printed letter rather than a person's nature

explanation.surface: Someone is judged dishonest in nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests personality and 'upright' honesty; here they are a printed letter and its slope.
explanation.definitionFit: Slanting typeface letters lean to the right, so each printed letter is not vertical.

clue.text: Boys possessing nothing or a great deal?

indicators.note: possessing means the boys' word holds the zero within it

parts.note: lads are boys
O, the figure zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: A question of whether boys own nothing at all or plenty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possessing' puts O (nothing) inside LADS.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, heaps or lots mean a great deal of something, so the plural noun matches.

clue.text: Storyteller needs the drink served up before work

indicators.note: served up in a down clue means the word is turned upwards, written backwards

parts.note: the drink is slang for the sea
op, short for opus, means a work

explanation.surface: A raconteur wants a drink poured before getting to work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served up' reverses SEA (the drink) to AES in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: He was the Greek teller of fables, so an ancient storyteller.

clue.text: Survival skills in the cunning devices of two US Presidents?

parts.note: George H. W. Bush and George W. Bush both share this surname
craft means cunning or guile, its trickery

explanation.surface: It suggests the wily schemes of a pair of American leaders were lessons in survival.
explanation.walkthrough: Two presidents share the surname Bush, father and son; the clue presents their craft as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Knowledge of how to live off the land in the wild is exactly a set of survival skills.

clue.text: Writer, for example, enthralled by unusual sites

indicators.note: enthralled means held captive, so the example word is held inside the shuffled letters
unusual signals the letters of sites are put into a different order

parts.note: say is used to introduce an example, as in 'a city, say'

explanation.surface: An author, for one, finds themselves captivated by odd locations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges the letters of sites into ESIST before SAY goes inside; 'for example' looks like it introduces the writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who composes short prose pieces on a subject is a kind of writer.

clue.text: Like dry wine, a litre that's beastly

parts.note: brut describes very dry champagne or sparkling wine

explanation.surface: Someone describes a litre of very dry wine as positively nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: Brut is the label term for the driest sparkling wines.
explanation.definitionFit: Savage and cruel are the senses shared, as in behaviour fit for a wild animal.

clue.text: Record call that is getting to the point?

parts.note: to tape something is to record it
to ring is to telephone, to call

explanation.surface: A recorded phone call that finally comes to the matter in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads literally: narrowing towards a sharp tip, not coming to the main issue.
explanation.definitionFit: Something narrowing gradually towards a tip is literally coming to a point.

clue.text: Material is wonderful and sumptuous, not hard

parts.note: fab, short for fabulous, means wonderful

indicators.note: not means the letter for hard is left out of the sumptuous word

parts.note: rich means lavish or sumptuous
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A cloth is praised as fabulous and luxurious, yet soft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes H (hard, as on pencils) from RICH.
explanation.definitionFit: Woven cloth or textile is the material meant, as used for clothes.
